en: Appendix I, Supplement 1,
was written by Vibhūticandra himself on paper folios at the end of the manuscript.
1.1.2 a...thā (thus)
To the question, "Why does he explain the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* according to the method of a *vārttika* [commentary] rather than as an independent treatise (*śāstra*) itself?
he says "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*), and so forth;
this is the meaning.

Out of concern and compassion, my mind has developed a desire to provide an exposition of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*; for this treatise composed by Dignāga is beneficial, yet it is being explained here word by word due to the deficiencies of the audience.

"Generally" (*prāyaḥ*) means for the most part. "Attached to the vulgar" (*prākṛtasaktaḥ*) refers to one whose lineage is base due to inferior knowledge. The treatises of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), which contain corruptions of the teachers' ethical systems, are "of a base lineage" because they originate from perverted knowledge. Furthermore, they are "vulgar" (*prākṛta*) for other reasons as well; "attachment to them" (*saktiḥ*) means devotion to those [treatises]. To the question "Why is he attached to the vulgar? he says:
Because he possesses weak intellect (*pratibalaprajña*), he discards even well-spoken words by treating them as ill-spoken;

and precisely because his intellect is weak, being unable to understand the well-spoken words of the teacher correctly on his own, he perceives them as faulty, thereby becoming indifferent to those well-spoken words of the teacher and developing animosity toward the teacher himself.
Thus [the author] says "merely," and so forth.

Not only was he uninterested in the well-spoken words of his teacher, but being possessed by the stains of malice and envy, he even hated Dignāga— who had become one whose addiction to the practice of eloquent sayings had increased—
despite the fact that there is a connection even between those who are separated [in time].

Well-spoken is the hymn (*sūkta*), therein is its practice, therein is its passion increased, and therein indeed is excessive attachment. By this, he expresses the state of having accumulated merit and knowledge, because that alone is such [a state].

For that reason, by which one who is previously free from worldly aims (*anarthī*) becomes attached to the ordinary (*prākṛta*), he is liberated; it is not for the sake of helping others, but rather for the supreme (*param*). It is most excellent.
There is indeed some benefit indicated by the word "mostly" (prāyaḥ);
since "iti" signifies a reason,
we have no concern on that account.

"Even though this treatise possesses great significance, it will not be of benefit to many; how then may I make its purpose fruitful?"—this kind of malice toward the Teacher is another cause of misfortune. Therefore, by means of the Teacher’s conduct, one should generate great respect for him through the elucidation of the correct meaning [instead of the distorted meaning]. By the word "also" (*api*), compassion in the form of the desire to separate [beings] from suffering is indicated, as in the thought: "I shall turn people away from the causes of misfortune. Furthermore, by the second word "by means of" (*iti*), he states that reflection and compassion are the causes [of the treatise].

Thus, through his reflection and compassion, his mind has long been bound by a persistent longing for the composition of the *Vārttika*— which serves as an exposition of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*— and his desire has proceeded continuously;
this is [the meaning] in the verse beginning with "prāyaḥ prākṛte" (1.2).
This he said.

This compendium has been undertaken here by the author of the treatise to be explained; therein, first, the half-verse of salutation, which is worthy of explanation, has been explained in the second chapter.
In the third chapter, however, the definition of perception along with its divisions has been analyzed according to its true nature through the removal of all doubts.
Now, having reached its proper occasion, inference [is to be discussed].
And that [teaching] is twofold:
for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others;
of these, the former has already been explained at the very beginning.

First, the purpose of that exposition was stated by the phrase "because the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful depends upon inference" (*anumānāyattatvāt*); for it has been explained [therein] that even perception (*pratyakṣa*) acquires its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) solely through the power of inference, and so forth.

As for the sūtra to be explained, it is the definition of inference stated in the second chapter of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*: "Inference is the cognition of an object through a three-featured logical mark" (*anumānaṃ dvidhā trirūpaliṅgato 'rthadṛk*), and so on.

Having explained that "inference for the sake of others" (*parārthānumāna*), defined as "the illumination of an object perceived by oneself," and so forth—as set forth in the third chapter [of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*]—by means of the fourth chapter of the *Vārttika*, this indeed constitutes the sequential indication of the first and subsequent chapters of the *Vārttika*.

Furthermore, the *Vārttika* consists of specific expositions and the like, according to the definition stated: "The *Vārttika* is the pointing out of an inconsistency in the *Sūtras* and the refutation thereof, which is the specific exposition. This very meaning has been expressed by others as follows: where a refutation is provided after having raised a fault in the *Sūtras*.

And since it is proclaimed that "the Vārttika is also a specific injunction," the author of the treatise said, "because it is to be communicated to another," and so forth, in order to explain the phrase "the word for the object seen by oneself" within the Sūtra.
The meaning of *svārtha* is stated in the commentary as follows:

"for one's own sake" (*svasmai idam*) is *svārtham*. This is not a *nitya-samāsa* (invariably compoundable term), and because it possesses all genders, it is a *caturthī-samāsa* (compound with the dative case) according to the rule;
the meaning is "one's own purpose."
That cognition by which one understands for oneself what is to be inferred is "for one's own sake" (*svārtha*);

that by which one communicates this to others through the statement of the three-fold logical mark (*trirūpavacana*) is "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*). [Objection: But was it not stated that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory? And inference is a means of valid cognition; how then can it be a verbal statement? [Response: There is no fault, because it is used in a figurative sense (*upacāra*). In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), however, it is cognition alone that is the determiner here as well, since it is cognition itself that is indicated by the statement of the three-fold logical mark.
For it is by means of words alone that another is awakened, not by means of one's own knowledge;
and since there is great doubt on the part of others regarding this matter, it is here being analyzed.

Since *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself) has now reached its proper occasion, and because it is the most proximate [topic] following the sequence of connection, the author first explains the two preceding words. By doing so, through the investigation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he has established the fourth chapter of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* as the "Investigation of the Example" (*Dṛṣṭāntavicāra*), and by means of the explanation of "Exclusion of Others" (*anyāpoha*), he has supported the fifth chapter as the "Investigation of Exclusion of Others" (*Anyāpohavicāra*). This is because all linguistic usage involving qualifiers and qualificands (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) and so forth is applicable only to the exclusion of others.

With the words "The fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsas) follow after that," the teacher Devendrabuddhi establishes the sixth chapter, which is the investigation of the fallacies of the reason. While providing a connection between the preceding and following chapters, he speaks also of the connection of the meaning of the first chapter in order to facilitate the understanding of his students and to state the body of the *Pramāṇavārttika* while refuting potential objections.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ācāryīye," this is the doubt raised here: if the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* was intended by the teacher Dharmakīrti to be explained, then let that very work be explained; why, instead, did he set it aside at the outset and explain the definition of inference (*anumāna*)?
The rebuttal to this begins with the words "of the Teacher" (*ācāryīya*) and so forth.

Here, "the Teacher" refers to Dignāga; for it is the treatise on the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa-śāstra*) composed by him—which elucidates the nature of perception and inference and is titled *Pramāṇasamuccaya*—that is being undertaken here to illuminate. Having removed the various types of [faults] from that work, specifically those found in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) by the earlier author of the sub-commentary (*vārtika*) which contained incorrect explanations and the contradictions of non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*), [Dharmakīrti] provides an explanation according to the [text's] actual state in the form of a *vārtika*.

The basis for that [conventional reality] is inference (*anumāna*), not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the latter is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) due to its having as its object the differentiation of things that are inexpressible, and thus it is useful only for its own [immediate] purpose.
In inference, however, she is established for the sake of dispelling all doubt, since by means of this [inference], the nature of the thing as it exists, unerring, is made known.

"Having established" (*vyavasthāpya*) means having previously established her specifically through the proclamation of the logical connection (*pratibandha*) by way of the three characteristics (*trirūpatā*).

For by the suffix *-tva* in *pūrvakālabhāvitva*, its occurrence at a prior time is made known; thus, the anticipated objection is refuted, and its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is indicated. Indeed, inference—by virtue of having its three characteristics well-ascertained and being conceptual in nature—is an absolute determiner and is therefore intrinsically valid. By this very [inference], the removal of all disagreements, the defeat of non-Buddhist opponents (*tīrthika*), the establishment of the meaning of the words of the authoritative teacher (*āpta*), and the proof of omniscience are accomplished, and not by perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This very point was established previously: even for perception, the ascertainment of its validity occurs solely by virtue of this [subsequent cognition],
because the nature of being a perception is possible even in a semblance of it, since the nature of consciousness and the objective form...

Furthermore, since a cognition with a clear manifestation can occur even in the case of the knowledge of two moons due to its being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), it is not possible for inference to possess the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) ascertained within its own appearance. Therefore, the validity of perception must be determined solely by means of the purity of the causes that constitute the inference.

Even though perception proceeds toward its object as soon as it is sought, it nevertheless perceives the form of the object as it truly is—having distinguished that form through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of repeated engagement in practical activity. Thus, this [perception] is preceded by inference, because positive and negative concomitance are themselves of the nature of inference.

Furthermore, it is observed that through the excellence of practice, perception arises as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) from the very moment it occurs, just like the cognition of gems, silver, and so forth; such [perception] is valid by itself, because the cause of error has been eliminated precisely by practice.

Otherwise, how could the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) be a valid means of knowledge? However, in certain cases where it is incapable of removing the causes of error, there is no certain conclusion (*niścaya*) regarding that [object] through inference; this was stated previously. But is it not the case that inference also has perception as its precursor? This restriction is not absolute, because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained by means of inference.
For it is not the case that perception perceives this restriction—that the pervader exists only where there is pervasion, or that the pervaded exists only where the pervader exists;

rather, even the logical mark (liṅga) is ascertained by a person only through the apprehension of its relationship. Thus, because it depends upon that relationship, that [perception] too is preceded by inference.
Furthermore, it has been stated that perception does not function at the time of the manifestation of inference;

indeed, it has also been stated that inference cannot occur with respect to its own manifestation in the same way that perception occurs with respect to its own manifestation. Therefore, because inference establishes the matter already mentioned, it was discussed first.

Alternatively, that treatise by which the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are characterized is a "treatise on characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śāstra*). It is the Tripiṭaka and it is authoritative (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-deceptive; thus, it is both a treatise on characteristics and an authoritative treatise. The teaching of the Blessed One is such an authoritative treatise on characteristics, unlike the deceptive and non-characterizing treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This is the intended meaning: for the word of the Blessed Ones is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇopapanna*) and makes known the nature of things such as impermanence. Alternatively, "authoritative" refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of these two has been pointed out by the Blessed One himself.

As it has been stated in the Abhidharma: "A person endowed with visual consciousness cognizes blue, but does not [cognize] 'it is blue'; by this, non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), which is sensory cognition, is described.
But one endowed with mental consciousness cognizes blue as 'it is blue.'"
Here, by the first [term], non-conceptual mental perception (*mānasa-nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is stated; by the second, however, conceptual mind (*vikalpaka-manas*) is stated;

and consciousness (*saṃvitti*) is expressed by the word "knows" (*jānāti*), for that which is not self-luminous cannot illuminate another, like an external light. There is also a specific statement to this effect: "knowledge has the nature of experience" (*anubhavarūpaṃ jñānam*).
The knowledge of the yogi is also described in that very same [text] through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
however, the definition of inference based on effect is stated as:
"Fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane."
"The lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by its signs"—this is the definition of the essential cause (*svabhāvahetu*).
"Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent; their nature is to arise and perish."

"For having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss"—here, the fact that the property to be proven (the *sādhyadharma*) is necessarily concomitant with the mere existence of that [subject] is stated; thus, this is stated as an essential nature (*svabhāva*). That by which it is taught through the word of the Blessed One is the scripture (*śāstra*), which is speech teaching the characteristics of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that inference (*anumāna*), which serves as the basis for the commentary on the *Ācāryīya-pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa-śāstra*—that is, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) taught by the Blessed One and explained by the Master Dignāga in his *Pramāṇasamuccaya*—is established first in this *Vārtika* for the sake of the purpose already stated.

Since it is the case that everywhere the virtuous proceed by first offering salutation whenever the occasion arises, the Teacher has stated this verse of salutation to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* for the sake of following good custom and for the sake of pacifying obstacles;
for through salutation there is an accumulation of merit,
and that [merit] wards off evil due to their mutual opposition.
Furthermore, as evil is being turned back, it also removes its own effect, which is an obstacle; thus, [the treatise] becomes a pacifier of obstacles.

Since the inference based on the Blessed One’s authority was just explained, the commentary on the verse of salutation, which has now reached its proper occasion, follows: "Having bowed to Him who is the embodiment of authority, who seeks the welfare of the world, the Sugata, the Protector, I shall compose this treatise."
"In order to establish the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a compendium (*samuccaya*) will be composed from my own [various] works, gathering here under one head what was scattered;
thus [is the purpose of] this *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
(1.1) Thus [it is said].

Having bowed to the one who has become the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhūta*), who seeks the welfare of the world, the Teacher, the Sugata, the Protector—to establish the means of valid cognition, this *Compendium* (of my own views) will be composed by gathering together what is scattered here and there.

In that regard, just as direct perception and other means of valid cognition reveal an unapprehended object useful for human goals and are consistent with reality, so too is the Blessed One supreme; for when the ultimate human goal is dependent upon the reality characterized by the four noble truths, it is by attaining knowledge having that as its object that those seeking liberation achieve liberation.

For the Blessed One alone—and no other—is the illuminator and non-contradictory [authority] regarding that which has not yet been realized; thus, by virtue of sharing the characteristics of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he is a "become" (*bhūta*) means of valid cognition, meaning one who has arisen.

The word "become" (*bhūta*) is for the purpose of negating things such as Īśvara, which are imagined by others to be eternal and have not yet come into being. Its actual meaning, however, is understood through implication; therefore, it will be explained that this [word "become"] is not intended for that [purpose of negation].
"He is both a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and has come into being (*bhūta*)," thus he is "one who has become a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇabhūta*).
It should be construed as: "having bowed down to him, the one who has become a means of valid cognition.
Now, since he is the object being pervaded by the action of bowing, the accusative case ought to be used here; so how is it that the dative case is employed?
Nor is this [suffix] applicable in connection with the word *namaḥ*, because it is not prescribed for that [word] when it is a noun ending in *s*;
nor is it present in the form *praṇamya* ending in the suffix *lyap*,
because that portion ending in *lyap* does not convey [the meaning of the base] and because it does not end in *s*.

It is said that the inclusion of the word "action" (*kriyā*) must also be made, according to the statement of Kātyāyana; thus, as in the example *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband"), the dative case is used here.
However, the author of the Bhāṣya has described the meaning of this rule in this way: [the dative is used when the action is for the sake of the recipient].

When there is a desire to express the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) for that which is being favored by the act of bowing—which has acquired the designation of an object (*karman*) because it is most desired to be attained through actions such as prayer and resolve—the dative case is used here.
However, when the action itself is intended to be expressed without its involvement in another action, then the accusative case is used for the object;
and thus, relying on this principle, the rule beginning with *gatyarthakarmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.12) has been rejected.

By this very reasoning, the second and fourth [cases] are established; nor is there an over-extension [of the rule], because correctness is observed elsewhere as well through the restriction of intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), based on following the usage of the learned and relying on worldly intention. For example, in forms such as *brumaḥ* (we say), the *parasmaipada* ending occurs; otherwise, since "the fruit of the action accrues to the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*) would apply, the *ātmanepada* ending would result here.
For the speaker, while uttering a statement to inform another, becomes connected with the fruit of the action; thus, the application of the *ātmanepada* would be mandatory in this case.

However, when utterance is intended without the exclusion of non-utterance—that is, when the intention is merely "we do not not speak, but rather we do speak"—then the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is entirely appropriate; thus there is no fault. Furthermore, according to the view of the author of the Sūtras, the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) is consistent with the underlying meaning here as well: the composer of the hymn, by means of devotion of body, speech, and mind, makes the Blessed One his own and offers himself to the Blessed One; thus he "gives."

Since there is a state of being pleased by the act of salutation, which is the object of the action, it is logically correct that the fourth case (dative) is used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*); thus, even according to the opinion of the three sages, the grammatical correctness [of the term] *jagaddhitaiṣiṇe* is not contradicted. Regarding *jagaddhitaiṣiṇe*: "the welfare of the world" (*jagaddhita*) refers to the absolute giving away and taking up of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; [it means] "to one whose nature is to desire that. Having bowed—that is, having performed a prostration with body, speech, and mind—to him, the connection is that "that collection will be composed. By this, worship through prostration is enjoined.
Regarding the word *śāstre*: according to the Uṇādi-sūtra "tṛn-tṛcau śaṃsi-kṣadādibhyaḥ saṃjñāyāṃ ca aniṭau," there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
*Śāsana* is the instruction on the means for the destruction of suffering;
and here, that is intended in its state as the cause (*hetv-avasthā*).

By the term "to the Sugata," the state of fruition (phalāvasthā) is designated; thus, the Blessed One, while acting as the Teacher (śāstṛ), is referred to by the word "Teacher" during his stage as a Bodhisattva. However, in the middle [of the verse], having paid homage to both states through the act of salutation (namaskāra), he speaks of them.
And these two states consist of cause and fruit; the causal state (hetvavasthā), moreover, consists of intention (āśaya) and application (prayoga).
The intention (*āśaya*) is also twofold: having the protection of all sentient beings as its form and having awakening (*bodhi*) as its objective support (*ālambana*).

The application (*prayoga*) is also twofold: that which pertains to the practice of liberation (*vimukti-caryā-bhāvī*) and that which pertains to the stages (*bhūmi-gata*). Regarding the stage of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), there is the preparatory application (*prāyogika*) consisting of generosity and the other perfections; however, on the [actual] stages, they are the matured (*vaipākika*) ones known as the perfections (*pāramitā*).
These are also twofold, distinguished by being "with effort" (*sābhisaṃskāra*) or "without effort" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

For seven stages are "with effort," because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) proceeds therein by the power of mental application (*ābhoga*) and signs (*nimitta*). Among those, in the seventh stage, the sign ceases, though not the mental application, because the apprehension of signs still persists. In the eighth stage, however, even the mental application ceases; since both have ceased upon reaching the stage of purity (*śuddhibhūmi*), the meditative concentration becomes one that flows spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*).
That by whose power one becomes the accomplisher of the welfare of the entire world,
the instructor of all for the sake of attaining all forms of consciousness—

this is the causal state (*hetvavasthā*) of the Blessed One, which begins from the initial generation of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) and extends up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), consisting of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
The fruit is the eleventh stage;
awakening (bodhi) is the knowledge of destruction and non-arising.
And the causal state, from the very beginning, is superior to all others because it is distinguished by the fourfold perfection.
The fourfold perfection— consisting of the practice of the entire accumulation of merit and knowledge, uninterrupted practice, long-term practice, and respectful practice—

produces in this very life a perfection of excellence in qualities that is unsurpassed through the practice of poetry, treatises, arts, and so forth; such a perfection is inconceivable even for others.

In that way, even by means of the roots of virtue acquired in a single lifetime, one attains the excellence of the supreme perfection of the eightfold sovereign powers and so forth among the gods and other realms; how much more so for one who has attained mastery, whose accumulations of merit and wisdom are being augmented through the practice of countless other eons—will such a person not attain the highest perfection?
This is not impossible, for as the cause becomes distinguished, the effect also becomes distinguished; thus, the perfection of the fruit is also distinguished in four ways.
Due to the possession of the fourfold perfection consisting of abandonment, knowledge, the form-body, and majesty,
the perfection of abandonment is also described as fourfold:
the abandonment of all defilements, absolute abandonment, and the abandonment of the obscurations to all meditative concentrations and attainments.
The perfection of knowledge is also distinguished by four aspects:
knowledge of all things, untaught knowledge, and non-dual knowledge.
The perfection of the form body is also fourfold: the perfection of the marks, consisting in the attainment of the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The perfection of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana-saṃpat*) consists in the attainment of the eighty secondary marks;
the perfection of having a body with bones as hard as adamant (*vajrasārāsthi-śarīratā-saṃpat*) consists in being endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa and possessing a firm, indestructible body.
The perfection of power is also fourfold:
the perfection of mastery over the creation, transformation, and sustaining of external objects;
and the perfection of mastery over the relinquishing and sustaining of life-span.
The perfection of mastery— consisting in the ability to traverse vast distances through unobstructed space with speed, and the power to enter into small and large spaces—
and the perfection of all phenomena characterized by various inherent wonders,
as well as the perfection of benefit, which exists in both states, are distinguished as being fourfold.

He is called the Sugata because his nature is the complete liberation from the suffering of cyclic existence and the three lower realms through the turning of the wheel of Dharma; or because he establishes [beings] in the three vehicles and the happy migrations, he is the Sugata—one who has gone well (*suṣṭhu gataḥ*) or attained [the goal], having abandoned everything that is to be abandoned in every respect and possessing the perfection of knowledge and so forth; or alternatively, he is the Sugata because he has gone beautifully (*śobhanaṃ vā gataḥ*), meaning he has perfectly awakened.
In this context, "attainment" (gati) refers to gnosis (*jñāna*), whereas in the previous [verse] it was used in the sense of "reaching.
By this [term], the state of the perfection of one's own welfare existing at the stage of fruition is described;

however, the previous [verse] described the perfection of the welfare of others existing at the causal stage. Now, he speaks of the incomparable perfection of the welfare of others existing at the stage of fruition.
Regarding the word *tāyine*:
that by which one is protected is *tāya*, namely the instruction on the well-seen path;
he who possesses this is *tāyī*.

Since those who act with discernment are occupied with a purpose, he states the immediate purpose [of this work] as "for the sake of establishing the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasiddhyai*), that is, for the sake of the systematic exposition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyutpatti*). [Objection: This [work] need not be commenced because it has its own purpose, since the establishment of the means of valid cognition has already been accomplished by [treatises such as] the *Nyāyamukha* and others.

Having raised the objection regarding a contradiction with the pervader (*vyāpakavirodha*)— namely, that what has already been established there is being established again, as in the example "cooked rice is cooked"—
he says "from his own doctrine having spread forth," using the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

For the meaning of this extensive treatise is difficult to comprehend; therefore, it has been established here in one place for the sake of easy understanding by way of removing all points of disagreement. Thus, there is no fault of redundancy.
The suffix *-tas* in the word *ekataḥ* is used in the sense of the locative case (*ekatra*).

Furthermore, since this verse occurs in the context of stating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it should be understood as establishing the authority of the Blessed One through both direct and reverse order.
The Blessed One is an authority because he seeks the welfare of the world;
and because he seeks the welfare of the world, he is a teacher; and because he is a teacher and, by virtue of his lineage, belongs to the class of the wise, he is the Sugata.
And because he is a Sugata, he is the protector of the entire world; therefore, "he is an authority" (*pramāṇa*)—this is the explanation in direct order (*anuloma*).
In reverse order (*pratiloma*), however: he is an authority because he is a protector (*tāyin*); he is a protector because he is a Sugata.
And that [is established] because of his being the Teacher,
and this [is established] because of his desiring the welfare of the world; thus,
there is a difference in interpretation based on the inference of the cause from the effect.

Therefore, in this verse, the author of the treatise has, in the first half, set aside the five words beginning with "having bowed" (*praṇamya*) and explained them through this section; he does not explain them further because they are easily understood.
Thus, he says that this is an "explanation of the verse" (*ślokavyākhyā*), since it consists of explaining those portions of the verse that require explanation.
Furthermore, while praise for other deities generally consists of superimposed qualities,
the praise of the Blessed One consists of incomparable, truly great qualities; thus, even those who are hostile are moved toward him, and those who are neutral become filled with faith.
Those who have faith become exceedingly increased in their devotion therein;
thus, there is an accumulation of merit for the composer of the hymn and for others,
and for the commentator as well, everything is accomplished in the same way.

For it is not the case that only he who acts with certainty is a person who acts with foresight.

Likewise, the object of inference is precisely *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), because it establishes merely that entity which is excluded from what possesses the opposite form; it is not a universal (*sāmānya*) of the nature—whether distinct or non-distinct—as imagined by others. As for the nihilists (*nāstika*), they maintain that [the self] is not distinct from the great elements (*mahābhūta*); indeed, they say this: consciousness (*caitanya*) is merely a specific manifestation of the great elements themselves, like the power of intoxication (*mada-śakti*). A person whose nature is such a body—that is, a body in which consciousness has manifested—is described as being "of such a nature."
Subsequently, there is a *dvandva* compound with the word "ghaṭa" (pot). This is either a dual form of the genitive or locative case used for selection (*nirddhāraṇa*),
or it is a genitive case expressing the relationship between a part and a whole.
Furthermore, the term "second" (*dvitīya*) means existing together with a second entity, such as either a jar or a person.
And by means of this pretext, he attempts to prove through formal argument (*prayoga*) that consciousness (*caitanya*) is not distinct from the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

For in the example, it is established in a general sense that a wall—which is non-originated—exists as "accompanied by a second" (*sadvitīya*) with respect to either a jar; and since being accompanied by a second is established even when there is only one, the example is not actually conjoined with the property to be proven (*sādhya*).

Likewise, even when taking the entire class of jars as the subject (*pakṣa*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*), it is improper for that very jar to be "accompanied by another" (*sadvitīya*). Thus, even when the proof is formulated in general terms, the mind considers that "being accompanied by such a person" is established through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Regarding the passage beginning with "here," etc.: even if such a person is not explicitly mentioned, because the probandum (*sādhya*) is pervaded by [the proponent's] intention, and because that [person] is unestablished (*asiddha*), there is the fault of non-concomitance (*ananvaya*) in the example.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the generality of the probandum" (*sādhyasāmānyena*):

it is argued that the jar’s being accompanied by a second entity is established by a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of exactly that kind—a person—because two faults would arise in relation to a specific [person]; however, since what is intended to be stated of the subject (*dharmin*) is merely that it is accompanied by a second entity in a general sense (*sāmānyena*), namely as either one or the other, this is not a fault. This argument is worthless, because the generality itself does not exist.
For [the subject] must be accompanied by a second entity, either by the pot or by the aforementioned person.

In that case, since the pot is adopted as the locus (*āśraya*) because it is the subject of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*), it cannot be "accompanied by a second" by virtue of this [person], because there is no difference [between them]; for being "accompanied by a second" is based on a distinction [between entities]. Nor can it be [accompanied] by the person, due to the fault of lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*).

He states this very point in the passage beginning with "that very generality is not established," and so forth: according to the manner described, the opponent does not accept that [the self] is distinct from the bodies because of defects such as the lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*).
He states that the same applies here regarding destruction as well:

for just as a jar’s being accompanied by another jar is established as the probandum because it is contradictory [to its own existence], and there is no suspicion of non-concomitance with such a person, and thus the proof is made through a generality due to the absence of both [contradiction and non-concomitance], so it is here too.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the distinction of the word 'jar'" and so forth:

the impermanence of sound is not the property to be proven (*sādhya*) in the case of the word [itself], because of the suspicion that there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*); nor is the impermanence of the jar the property to be proven in the case of the word, because it is impossible.
Furthermore, if the impermanence of a jar were known with respect to sound, there would be a contradiction with one's own tenets (*abhyupetavirodha*),
because the impermanence of a jar is not admitted in the case of sound;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is also a contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*), since a property belonging to one thing is being predicated of another.
Furthermore, if one conceives [the reason] based on a difference in terminology, there is the fault of the example being devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*),
because destruction in general is established even by means of a non-existent destruction, provided that no specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣa*) is grasped.

Regarding the phrase "tadvataḥ" (of that which possesses it), meaning of that which possesses destruction, we have already stated that there is no deficiency in the application of the property of being accompanied by another (*sadvitīyatva*) in its very own manner; however, you have misconstrued it in an entirely different way and thereby attempted to show that the fault is equal [in both cases].
To explain this, he says "na hi" and so forth.

The property of being "either one or the other" (*anyatarārthāntaratva*) as a universal (*sāmānya*) has been rejected because it is presented [as a reason] in both the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), namely the jar, and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), namely the wall; for the opponent intends the probandum (*sādhya*) to reside either in the subject of the thesis or in the subject of the example—meaning that the probandum is either the property of being "either one or the other" residing in the subject of the thesis, or that same property residing in the subject of the example.

"How can there be 'diversity' when diversity exists? [To this we reply: It is not the case here that the property of being a different object (*arthāntaratva*) belonging to the wall is what is to be proven (*sādhya*) in the pot, nor is it intended that the property of the pot is what is to be proven in the wall. We do not say that there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) or similar faults such that there would be an equal defect [in our argument]. Rather, such a thing is simply the property to be proven. For instance, with respect to the previously mentioned person and pot, the characteristic of being a different object from one another, when examined, is not established;
for the pot's state of being a different object [from the person] is not [established] due to contradiction.

Because there is a suspicion that even the body lacks [the property], it is not accepted by him; thus, by this much in common, the word is established through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Since they maintain a non-connection with some form of impermanence, its connection is what is to be proven.
Similarly, if there were the existence of another object, the pot would also possess it; thus he says, "But the existence of one or the other as another object," in order to explain the sūtra.
The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction:
whereas non-eternality is a property of the thing itself (*vastudharma*), having a second (*sadvitīyatva*) is not a property of the thing itself,
because it is established by the force of [the proponent's] wish.

For this [property] is neither an effect nor an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the entity, since it is transferred by the force of one's will even though it is a different object; yet, because it exists [in the subject], the explanation of the statement "the pot possesses that" is "a pot accompanied by either one of the two.
The reason "vitality and so forth" is indeed conclusive.
Indeed, although knowability (*prameyatva*) is common to all things, for one who denies the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
it lacks concomitance; therefore, that [knowability] possesses an invariable positive concomitance only within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself.
He states the reason as being only that which follows [the probandum];
here too, how is there non-exclusion from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa),
or how is it that it exists only in the similar instance (sapakṣa)?

What is the fruit of a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) that possesses a similar class (*sapakṣa*), if the existence [of the reason] in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is not excluded? Or, if it is excluded, how can there be no negative concomitance (*avyatireka*)?
For negative concomitance is nothing other than the negation of existence;
and this [claim] is a contradiction.
"There is neither positive concomitance (anvaya) nor negative concomitance (vyatireka).

Indeed, that very negation of positive concomitance expressed as "not" is itself the negative concomitance; however, this leads back to the same point: because negative concomitance is impossible for that which is non-existent.

In this regard, it must further be stated: how can there be a negation of a connection (*anvaya*) for that which is non-existent? Indeed, a negation that draws out the nature of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*) would not be possible with respect to what is non-existent.
For the scope of the negative particle (*nañ*) is not exclusively exclusion (*paryudāsa*); what then? It is also absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
Even the refutation by means of perception does not apply,
for there is no contradiction with that [non-existence];
thus, even that [refutation] is not possible.

If it is argued that this is because there is no application of case-endings— such as those denoting location (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth— which indicate the object of a negation, the answer to this has already been stated;
therefore, there is no such thing as a "concomitant" (*anvayin*) reason.
And if it is argued that the nature of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) does not exist in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*),
because it has been stated that a property (*dharma*) is of three kinds— based on existence, non-existence, or both—
and that there can be no property whatsoever for a non-existent thing;
Is it not the case that this very absence of properties (*dharmaviraha*) is its property?

For properties are not merely the nature of a thing; even non-existent things are brought into this conventional usage by some particular context, otherwise there would be no conventional usage regarding them at all.
Furthermore, even for existing things, there is no relation of property and property-bearer from the perspective of ultimate reality;
it has been stated in the *Vārttika* that "it is merely the intellect that constructs a connection.
And when things do not exist, who can prevent a conjunction produced by the intellect?

Furthermore, the determinations of existence, non-existence, both, or neither for those who possess conventions regarding "that" and "not-that" would not be definitive means of proof if they were not grasped with certainty; therefore, those objects of cognition (*prameya*) must be stated by him as being determined in some way or other— even if it be [as] non-existence— for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not have only positive entities as its object.

Since the defining characteristic of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*), one should not establish [an object] through that [cognition] unless it is sublated by another [cognition] regarding its own object.
Therefore, since there exists the definition of other means of valid cognition, the object of cognition...
[is established] through the non-contradiction of intention. 11.2.11ab.
This will be explained in the commentary on the two verses beginning with "56. Of the light of a jewel and a lamp... and so forth.
Some say:

if, even though it is erroneous, the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-discrepant due to its correspondence with the object, then this would result in a third means of knowledge distinct from perception and inference, since [the definition of] a valid means of knowledge is stated as being "non-discrepant."
For instance, the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel is not perception, because it is erroneous and conceptual;
perception, however, is the opposite of that.
Nor is it inference, because it is not produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor is it invalid because of its correspondence with reality;
to this it is replied: this is indeed inference.
For it will be established immediately hereafter that the general definition of inference is:
"Inference is the cognition of an imperceptible object through another [perceptible] object, provided there is no lack of apprehension of the relationship [between them].
And in this case, because of the connection between the gem and its luster—since the latter is an effect of the former—an illusion of the gem arises with respect to that luster.
Therefore, because it arises from a sign that is an effect, this is indeed inference;
for instance, at first, a non-erroneous visual consciousness arises with respect to the luster of a jewel.

And by him, the essential nature of the effect as a logical mark has been understood; for it is established that only the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is the logical mark, and its capacity to signify arises through identity and causality,
whereas a conceptualized form possesses no otherness [from the real].
If it is asked, "How can there be a positive concomitance (anvaya) with a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), given that either identity (tādātmya) or causality (tadutpatti) must exist?
we do not say that it is with that very same [particular], but rather with another particular of the same class.
And so it has been said:
"For even that which belongs to the same class, when there is an intention to express non-difference, is indeed called 'that very same thing'.

Therefore, it is the individual particulars (svalakṣaṇas) of the same class themselves—when they are considered in their entirety as being delimited by the exclusion of dissimilar things—that are called a "universal" (sāmānya).

Even where properties such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and so forth are established, the distinction between the property and the property-bearer (dharma-dharmin) is intended merely as a means for instructing the ignorant;
the indicative mark (liṅga) that brings about cognition is the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) itself.
Thus he said:

If it is argued that the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is merely conceptual and not real, such that the cognition arising from the mark (*liṅga*), namely smoke, as the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) does not proceed by superimposing the smoke itself [upon the object], but rather upon another location; whereas the illusion of a jewel (*maṇi-bhrānti*), however, superimposes the possessor of the mark upon the mark known as the "luster of a jewel" (*maṇiprabhā*)—[we reply: The distinction between the property and the property-bearer is indeed conceptual and not real. Nevertheless, when a cognition arises from the mark, smoke, regarding the possessor of the mark, it does not function by superimposing the smoke itself, but rather upon another location. However, the illusion of a jewel, while superimposing the possessor of the mark upon the mark called the "luster of a jewel," [does so] precisely because that luster is the very cause of the illusion of the jewel; for it is the luster of the jewel that produces the illusion of the jewel, and not the mere appearance of a flame. Thus, since the luster of the jewel is the cause of the illusion of the jewel, the superimposition of the possessor of the mark upon the mark is established. But in the case of smoke, there is no such thing as a "luster of smoke" which could serve as the cause of the illusion of fire. Therefore, the two cases are not analogous. Furthermore, the cognition of the possessor of the mark produced by smoke proceeds toward a specific location, whereas the cognition of the possessor of the mark produced by the luster of a jewel proceeds toward the jewel itself. Consequently, the two cognitions differ in their objects. Thus, the claim that the cognition of the possessor of the mark produced by smoke is like the cognition of the possessor of the mark produced by the luster of a jewel is untenable. Therefore, the distinction between the property and the property-bearer is not merely conceptual. Hence, the inference of fire from smoke is valid. This concludes the section on the establishment of the three-fold nature of the reason. Now follows the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence. If it is argued that the reason is not distinct from the thesis (*sādhya*), because the reason is merely a particular aspect of the thesis, and thus the reason is nothing other than the thesis itself, and therefore the reason cannot be a separate category of evidence—[we reply: This is not so. For the reason is a particular aspect of the thesis insofar as it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). However, the reason is not the thesis itself, because the thesis is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), whereas the reason is the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*). Since they are distinct, the reason is a separate category of evidence. Furthermore, if the reason were identical to the thesis, then just as the thesis is not perceived before it is proven, the reason would likewise not be perceived before the proof occurs. But this is not the case; for the reason is perceived prior to the proof. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Moreover, if the reason were identical to the thesis, then just as the thesis is not certain until proven, the reason would also be uncertain. But this is not the case; for the reason is certain. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Furthermore, if the reason were identical to the thesis, then just as the thesis is not established without the reason, the reason would likewise not be established without the thesis. But this is not the case; for the reason is established independently. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Consequently, the reason is a separate category of evidence. This concludes the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence. Now follows the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it is not perceived independently. If it is argued that the reason is not perceived independently of the thesis, and therefore the reason is not a separate category of evidence—[we reply: This is not so. For the reason is perceived independently of the thesis insofar as it is a property of the subject. However, the reason is not perceived independently of the thesis insofar as it is the means of proving that thesis. Since these two aspects are distinct, the reason is a separate category of evidence. Furthermore, if the reason were not perceived independently, then just as the thesis is not perceived without the reason, the reason would likewise not be perceived without the thesis. But this is not the case; for the reason is perceived even when the thesis is not yet known. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Moreover, if the reason were not perceived independently, then just as the thesis is not established without the reason, the reason would likewise not be established without the thesis. But this is not the case; for the reason is established through its own nature. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Consequently, the reason is a separate category of evidence. This concludes the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it is not perceived independently. Now follows the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it is not a different entity. If it is argued that the reason is not a different entity from the thesis, because the reason is merely a particular aspect of the thesis, and therefore the reason is nothing other than the thesis itself, and thus the reason cannot be a separate category of evidence—[we reply: This is not so. For the reason is a particular aspect of the thesis insofar as it is a property of the subject. However, the reason is not the thesis itself, because the thesis is the property to be proven, whereas the reason is the means of proof. Since they are distinct, the reason is a separate category of evidence. Furthermore, if the reason were identical to the thesis, then just as the thesis is not perceived before it is proven, the reason would likewise not be perceived before the proof occurs. But this is not the case; for the reason is perceived prior to the proof. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Moreover, if the reason were identical to the thesis, then just as the thesis is not certain until proven, the reason would also be uncertain. But this is not the case; for the reason is certain. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Furthermore, if the reason were identical to the thesis, then just as the thesis is not established without the reason, the reason would likewise not be established without the thesis. But this is not the case; for the reason is established independently. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the thesis. Consequently, the reason is a separate category of evidence. This concludes the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it is not a different entity. Now follows the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it is not a different locus. If it is argued that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it does not exist in a locus other than the subject, and therefore the reason is nothing other than the subject itself, and thus the reason cannot be a separate category of evidence—[we reply: This is not so. For the reason exists in a locus other than the subject insofar as it is a property of the subject. However, the reason does not exist in a locus other than the subject insofar as it is the means of proving that subject. Since these two aspects are distinct, the reason is a separate category of evidence. Furthermore, if the reason were not a separate category of evidence because it did not exist in a locus other than the subject, then just as the subject is not perceived without the reason, the reason would likewise not be perceived without the subject. But this is not the case; for the reason is perceived even when the subject is not yet known. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the subject. Moreover, if the reason were not a separate category of evidence because it did not exist in a locus other than the subject, then just as the subject is not established without the reason, the reason would likewise not be established without the subject. But this is not the case; for the reason is established through its own nature. Therefore, the reason is not identical to the subject. Consequently, the reason is a separate category of evidence. This concludes the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it is not a different locus. Now follows the refutation of the objection that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it is not a different time. If it is argued that the reason is not a separate category of evidence because it does not exist at a time other than the time of the thesis, and therefore the reason is nothing other than the thesis itself, and thus the reason cannot be a separate category of evidence—[we reply: This is not so. For the reason exists at a time other than the time of the thesis insofar as it is a property of the subject. However, the reason does not exist at a time other than the time of the thesis insofar as it is the means of proving that thesis. Since these two aspects are distinct, the reason is a separate category of evidence. Therefore, why should it not be lost?
Its status as being produced from a connection is indeed lost; we say only this much: that the error regarding the location is excessive here.

Let there be no validity in the case of [the cognition] "this is a jewel" with respect to that very spot; but who can prevent its being an inference when it brings about the acquisition of the mere jewel?

If it is argued that all inference is indeed accepted as erroneous because there is no recollection of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the case of the illusion of a gem, [we reply:

if such recollection is absent, inference does not thereby cease to be inference. For when one perceives fire from smoke instantaneously, without having recollected positive and negative concomitance, why is that cognition not accepted as inference?
We maintain that inference is simply that which arises from a mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics;
however, if the illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel is indeed an inference, for what purpose is it cited as an example?
For when the non-contradiction of inference in general is to be established, it is not logical for an instance of inference itself to serve as the example.

This too is not a fault, because although the illusion of the jewel (*maṇibhrānti*) is indeed an error, the opponent intends it merely as an instance of the speaker’s non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*).

However, other inferential signs such as smoke are non-erroneous and have the appearance of real entities; otherwise, they would lack non-correspondence. Therefore, the illusion of the jewel is adduced as an example.
To this we reply: this [explanation] is excessively cumbersome, difficult to establish, contradictory, inconsistent, and thus does not please the wise.

In the case of the cognition of a jewel regarding the luster of a jewel, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it does not produce a true object; it is neither perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor inference (*anumāna*) due to the absence of their respective characteristics.

For it is a well-established principle that whatever lacks the characteristic of a certain thing cannot be designated as being of that form, just as a cow cannot be designated as having the form of a horse.
Inference is the knowledge of the object to be inferred arising from a logical mark (liṅga) ascertained through its three characteristics;
in this case, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya),
for the concomitance "whatever is light is all a gem" is not established.
Nor is there a negative concomitance (vyatireka), such as "whatever is not a jewel is not its radiance," because the relationship of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva) is unestablished.
Nor can the cognition of the form of the jewel produced by the light be considered the subject (*pakṣa*), because it is false;

furthermore, one who has not grasped the relationship between the sign and the signified does not cognize the object of inference through the sign. Even one who cognizes it immediately without formal instruction must have previously grasped that relationship, since otherwise such a cognition would be impossible.

Nor does the luster of a gem appear as an effect of the gem in the same way that smoke appears as an effect of fire; for it appears only in the form of its cause and, being a cognizer [of that cause], it constitutes a certain logical mark (*liṅga*). It is not uncertain, unlike doubtful smoke, and there is no certainty here because it is a false cognition.

As for what was said— that at first, a non-erroneous visual consciousness arises with respect to the light, and by that the light's status as an effect is determined— this is an act of extreme temerity; for this is indeed sensory cognition, which, due to its clarity, is like the cognition of one who is detached from passion, yet it arises erroneously through defects of the sense organs and so forth, failing to distinguish the light from the form of the gem.
Furthermore, no aspect of light is perceived therein;
nor can an unperceived aspect serve as an objective support (*ālambana*), for that would entail the absurd consequence that everything could serve as an objective support.
Nor is this a mental error, because once the defects of the sense faculties have ceased, the object is again apprehended in its own true form.

Furthermore, there is no relation of identity (*tādātmya*) between the jewel and its radiance because they are distinct; and when the object has been apprehended, the validity or invalidity of the cognition is determined by that [object].

For indeed, no one's activity occurs without an object, and in this case, the cognition of the jewel has the radiance as its object, whereas the radiance is not the jewel. Thus, one who acts according to such a determination would not be successful.
Inference, however, never deviates from having the form of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, because it arises from a lack of reality, that false cognition is indeed erroneous; for the nature of a thing as excluded from what is dissimilar exists already in its general form, otherwise even the dissimilar would be that very thing. Thus, that mental image corresponds to the actual object.
However, in the case of a light, there is no nature of being a gem within the light itself that is excluded from the dissimilar, since the light has only the light itself as its objective support.
In inference, on the other hand, because it possesses the form of the inferable, it touches upon the actual object.
When there is a causal connection (*pratibandha*), there is validity; however, in the case of the light [of a gem], the cognition of the gem is not like this, and thus it is not an inference.

For this very reason, it is cited as an example—standing outside the subject (*pakṣa*) acknowledged by both the proponent and the opponent—in order to demonstrate the absolute greatness of the causal connection. Although it is of such a nature and non-discrepant, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*) it is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it is a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Therefore, the author of the treatise states:
"Even though there is no difference in being false cognitions, there is a distinction with respect to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."
He explains this very point:

for here, because of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), the apprehension of the light of a lamp as having the form of a gem is not distinguished from that [other case]; rather, this is indeed false cognition, like the cognition of a gem in the light of a lamp seen through the opening of a jar, a cloth, or a keyhole.
Having thus restated its status as false cognition, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
The word "api" (also/even) here signifies an excellence regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Thus, since the demonstration of validity here transgresses both the words of the author of the treatise and logical reasoning (*nyāya*), it is a mere display of deception; therefore, I desist from further consideration of this worthless argument.
Even so, when there is non-discrepancy [with perception], then inference is all the more free from contradiction.

1.37 Even though no new sentient beings appear and Buddhas are infinite throughout the three times, nevertheless, there is no exhaustion of *saṃsāra*, just as space is inexhaustible and boundless; for in every single direction, the stream of sentient beings is without end.

Even when the mind is directed elsewhere, one perceives a form with the eye; the non-apprehension of its conventional designation (saṃketa) is clear therein, and the conceptual construction (kalpanā) arising from it is that which employs a word denoting a universal, being co-referential with that [perceived object].

In the absence of non-conceptual [wisdom], how can there be the realization of specific distinctions? Those who have disregarded the reality of suchness, closing their eyes like an elephant, merely extend their investigation into external objects based solely on worldly intellect.

Or what contradiction is there if many [impressions], having produced an excellence (*atiśaya*), were individually to become the cause of cognition, just as the sense organs and so forth are? If it is asked,
"How can that which exists at a different time be an object of apprehension?", they [the proponents] understand its status as an object of apprehension.

Just as someone who has tasted salt water in one place knows that all salt water is likewise salty, and just as a skilled person, having observed smoke arising from a fire in a kitchen, understands that all such smoke is likewise produced by fire— so too, when certain things exist, the cognition of this [effect] arises from them.

Because that [substance] would be the cause [of its own perception], there would be an infinite regress of causes everywhere; for instance, just as there might be a determinative cognition (*avasāya*) produced by the mind (*pṛṣṭhaja*) regarding a jar— which is a composite of form, odor, taste, and touch— even when there is a visual perception grasping only the form.
An over-ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) is a determination (*vyavasāya*). Having seen a single instance of smoke, one determines that "everything possesses fire.

This is because one experiences the determination—arising with respect to that [smoke] as possessing [fire]—only by including within its scope the entire class of individuals excluded from everything other than that [smoke], based on the cognition: "By means of perception aided by non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), smoke has been determined by me to be produced from fire.

Just as when only color (*rūpa*) is seen by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), the conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) arising subsequently from its force determines: "A jar, which is a collection of color, odor, taste, and touch, has been seen by me."
In this case, if there were disagreement, the practical application of valid cognition would be destroyed; [this is] because of the authority of inference—
[the claim that] "he is omniscient"— is [untenable].
Direct perception—44;
inference for the sake of others—55.
